patterns.title: Chicken: The Cost of Refusing to Yield
patterns.domain: Strategic and game-theoretic problems; anti-coordination, concession, brinkmanship, and allocation authority

sources.title: University game-theory notes, section 3.3, Chicken
sources.supports: Preference ordering, anti-coordination best replies, pure equilibria, and Russell’s 1959 use of the driving analogy for brinkmanship.
sources.read_method: Chicken section and reproduced historical quotation read.
sources.boundary: Teaching explanation and historical quotation, not an empirical risk estimate. Article uses none of the notes’ broader claims about resource classifications, and no numerical payoffs are transferred.

sources.title: Rapoport and Chammah, The Game of Chicken (1966)
sources.supports: Early formal and experimental treatment of Chicken.
sources.read_method: Publisher bibliographic record and abstract read.
sources.boundary: Full text was not available through the accessed publisher page. No detailed result, sample, or effect estimate is attributed to unread text; the historical claim is limited to the verified early publication.

sources.title: Duffy and Feltovich, Do Actions Speak Louder Than Words?
sources.supports: Comparison of cheap talk, prior-action observation, and control across Chicken, Stag Hunt, and prisoner’s dilemma; relative informativeness depends on game structure.
sources.read_method: October 2000 author draft read, including game tables, round-robin procedures, and conclusions. Author publication page verifies 2002 Games and Economic Behavior 39, 1–27. Article and source annotation label the linked version explicitly.
sources.boundary: Primarily Pittsburgh undergraduates; 20 subjects per session, 10 rounds of each of three games, round-robin matching so each row player faced each column player once per game. Prior action was taken against another participant, not a binding current choice. Some differences between information treatments were not always significant; no quantitative effect or validation of the bridge-entry intervention claimed.

sources.title: University of Florida, The Hawk–Dove Game
sources.supports: Biological Hawk–Dove payoff structure and anti-coordination when fighting cost C exceeds resource value V.
sources.read_method: Teaching account of payoff matrix, C > V > 0, and fitness/population interpretation read.
sources.boundary: The 1973 foundational Nature paper was located but its scan was not text-readable in the web interface; no claim to having read it or new empirical claim is made. Article cites the readable university explanation, not an unread primary scan.

patterns.short_description: Recognize when each side hopes the other will concede while mutual refusal produces the worst outcome, then distinguish selecting who yields from changing the leverage created by refusal.
use_when: Why can shared fear encourage mutual refusal?
Ada and Karim face a hypothetical narrow-bridge concession game: press ahead or yield.
goals: Recognize the familiar predicament before specialist terminology.
Explain the defining mechanism and distinguish neighboring concepts.

Stipulated ordering: pass while other yields, mutual caution, yield alone, mutual pressing with collision risk. Two asymmetric equilibria; mutual pressing least preferred after accounting for risk; no quantified collision risk, actual road rule, or complete engineering specification.
Separate hypothetical behavior, model results, documented cases, and practical editorial proposals.
mechanisms: An authorized entry procedure admits one direction at a time, changing decision rights and available actions.
Control and usable waiting space are assumed. Equipment can fail; the diagram is not a traffic-engineering specification.
example_user_queries: Why can shared fear encourage mutual refusal?

visual.question: Why can shared fear encourage mutual refusal?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. Ada and Karim choose press ahead or yield. One pressing while the other yields gives the presser priority; both pressing creates collision risk and is stipulated to be the least-preferred combination for both. Both yielding represents mutual caution under the stipulated middle ranking. Double outlines mark the two asymmetric equilibria. Controlled entry changes the available actions. Change: Replace unrestricted competing entry with authorized, reliable priority control. Limitation: Control and usable waiting space are assumed. Equipment can fail; the diagram is not a traffic-engineering specification.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. The bridge is a classic hypothetical strategic illustration, not driving guidance. Each prefers pressing against yielding and yielding against pressing. Mutual pressing is stipulated to be least preferred, taking its risk into account; fear of a collision alone would not establish that ranking. Controlled entry changes decision rights; it does not make mutual yielding stable under the original incentives.
